subject: Civil Engineering
title: Schedule Compression: Crashing and Fast-Tracking
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Schedule Compression: Crashing and Fast-Tracking.

hook.text: The project is behind schedule. The deadline doesn't move. You need to accelerate.

buildup.text: Crashing adds resources to critical tasks — more workers, overtime, or extra shifts.

discovery.text: Fast-tracking overlaps tasks that were planned sequentially — starting construction before design finishes.

twist.text: Crashing costs more money. Fast-tracking adds risk — if design changes, rework multiplies.

climax.text: The Pentagon was fast-tracked during WWII — construction began before design was half complete.

punchline.text: Speed costs money or risk. The only free schedule acceleration doesn't exist.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of fast-tracking a construction project?
options: Workers become exhausted from overtime and make mistakes
Overlapping tasks means design changes can cause expensive rework
The project budget automatically doubles when tasks overlap

details.summary: Schedule compression reduces project duration using two primary techniques. Crashing adds resources to critical activities to shorten their duration at increased cost. Fast-tracking overlaps activities that were originally planned in sequence, accepting increased risk for schedule savings.
details.whyItMatters: When projects fall behind schedule, compression techniques offer options to recover time. Understanding their cost and risk implications prevents managers from making the problem worse.
takeaways: Crashing shortens duration by adding resources at increased direct cost
Fast-tracking overlaps sequential activities, increasing rework risk
Both techniques are applied to critical path activities for maximum effect

faq.question: How do you decide whether to crash or fast-track a project?
faq.answer: Crashing is preferred when additional resources can effectively shorten activities and the owner can absorb the extra cost. Fast-tracking is preferred when concurrent work is feasible without excessive rework risk. Often both are combined.

faq.question: What are the diminishing returns of crashing critical activities?
faq.answer: Adding resources to an activity eventually produces less schedule reduction per dollar spent. Beyond a point, additional workers create congestion and coordination overhead that offset productivity gains.
